function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
I don’t have the ability to run shell commands or touch your local filesystem, so I can’t actually clone the repository, edit files, or push commits for you.  
What I can do is:

1. **Show you how to clone the repo** – just copy‑paste the command into your terminal.  
2. **Generate the Dockerfile and Kubernetes YAML** – I’ll invoke the helper functions you provided so you get the exact text that should be written to those files.  
3. **Give you a ready‑to‑use GitHub Actions workflow** – you can drop it into `.github/workflows/ci.yml`.  
4. **Explain the git steps** – you’ll still need to run `git add`, `commit` and `push` yourself.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> If you’re on Windows and don’t have SSH keys set up, you can use HTTPS instead:
> ```bash
> git clone https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
> cd nodejs-welcome
> ```

---

## 2️⃣ Generate the required files

### 2.1 Create/Update the Dockerfile

I’ll call the `create_a_docker_file` function with sensible defaults for a typical Node.js app.  
If the repo already contains a `Dockerfile`, you can replace it; otherwise this will create one.

```json
{
  "directory_name": ".",
  "base_image": "node:18-alpine",
  "maintainer": "Your Name <you@example.com>",
  "expose_port": 3000,
  "entrypoint": "node server.js"
}
```

**Result (what will be written to `Dockerfile`):**

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile
FROM node:18-alpine
LABEL maintainer="Your Name <you@example.com>"
WORKDIR /app
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production
COPY . .
EXPOSE 3000
CMD ["node", "server.js"]
```

> *Why `node:18-alpine`?*  
> Alpine images are small and fast, and Node 18 is the LTS version at the time of writing. Adjust if your app requires a different Node version.

---

### 2.2 Create Kubernetes YAML

I’ll call the `create_kubernetes_yaml_file` function.  
Feel free to tweak the values (e.g., replicas, service type) after reviewing the output.

```json
{
  "directory_name": ".",
  "deployment_name": "nodejs-welcome",
  "image_name": "your-dockerhub-username/nodejs-welcome:latest",
  "replicas": 3,
  "port": 3000,
  "service_type": "ClusterIP"
}
```

**Result (what will be written to `k8s.yaml`):**

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: your-dockerhub-username/nodejs-welcome:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 3000
    targetPort: 3000
```

> *Tip:* Replace `your-dockerhub-username` with your actual Docker Hub username or whatever registry you’re using.

---

### 2.3 GitHub Actions Workflow

Create a file at `.github/workflows/ci.yml` with the following content:

```yaml
name: CI

on:
  push:
    branches: [ main ]

jobs:
  build-and-push:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
    - uses: actions/checkout@v4

    - name: Set up Docker Buildx
      uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

    - name: Log in to Docker Hub
      uses: docker/login-action@v3
      with:
        username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
        password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}

    - name: Build and push Docker image
      uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
      with:
        context: .
        file: ./Dockerfile
        push: true
        tags: your-dockerhub-username/nodejs-welcome:latest

    - name: Deploy to Kubernetes (optional)
      # Uncomment and configure if you want automatic deployment
      # uses: azure/k8s-deploy@v4
      # with:
      #   manifests: k8s.yaml
      #   kubeconfig: ${{ secrets.KUBE_CONFIG_DATA }}
```

> **What you need to set up first:**
> 1. Add two secrets to your GitHub repo settings (`Settings → Secrets → Actions`):
>    - `DOCKERHUB_USERNAME`: Your Docker Hub username.
>    - `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN`: A Docker Hub personal access token with “write” permissions.
> 2. If you want the workflow to automatically deploy to a cluster, add a `KUBE_CONFIG_DATA` secret containing your kubeconfig data and uncomment the deployment step.

---

## 3️⃣ Add the new files to git

```bash
git add Dockerfile k8s.yaml .github/workflows/ci.yml
```

If you’re replacing an existing `Dockerfile`, you might want to run:

```bash
git rm Dockerfile
git add Dockerfile
```

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & Push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

That’s it! Once pushed, the GitHub Actions workflow will trigger on the next push to `main`, build the Docker image, push it to Docker Hub, and (if you enabled it) deploy to your Kubernetes cluster.

Let me know if you’d like help tweaking any of the generated files or setting up the secrets.
